nameStory: The 'marbled' in this scud's name comes from its distinctive greyish color decorated with reddish-brown markings that create a mottled, marble-like pattern across its tiny body. Scuds get their common name from their quick, darting swimming motion that resembles a boat scudding across the water.
description: Marbled scuds are tiny marine crustaceans that look like miniature shrimp, growing up to about half an inch long. These greyish creatures are decorated with distinctive reddish-brown markings that give them their marbled appearance. They're tube-building amphipods, meaning they construct protective homes from bits of algae and debris glued together with their own silky secretions. You'll find them in the intertidal zone where they're part of the fouling community that grows on docks, rocks, and other underwater surfaces.

idTips.label: Marbled coloration
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive greyish body decorated with reddish-brown patches and markings that create a mottled, marble-cake appearance

idTips.label: Tube structures
idTips.description: Search for small, irregular tubes made of algae fragments and debris bits that feel slightly slimy from the mucus that holds them together

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: These tiny crustaceans reach about 10 millimeters (less than half an inch) long, making them easy to overlook without close inspection

idTips.label: Shrimp-like body
idTips.description: The body appears flattened from side to side with multiple pairs of legs, giving it a compressed, shrimp-like profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Clustered occurrence
idTips.description: Found in groups or colonies rather than alone, often creating patches of tubes on surfaces that feel bumpy and encrusted to the touch

habitat: Marbled scuds live in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in areas with moderate wave action. You'll find them attached to dock pilings, rocks, seawalls, and other hard surfaces where fouling communities develop. They prefer areas that get regular submersion and exposure with the tides, typically in the mid to lower intertidal zones.

seasonality.spring: Active reproduction begins, and you may notice fresh tube construction as populations expand. Look for new, lighter-colored tubes among the established colonies.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with largest populations visible. Tubes are most abundant and obvious during summer low tides when intertidal areas are exposed.
seasonality.fall: Populations remain active but may begin to decline. Older tubes start to look more weathered and darker from accumulated algae and sediment.
seasonality.winter: Reduced activity but still present. Many individuals remain in their tubes, making them less obvious but still detectable during winter low tides.

funFact: Marbled scud males come in two completely different forms with opposite life strategies - the large 'fighter' males that battle for mates, and the small 'sneaker' males that slip past the fighters to secretly mate while the big guys are distracted!
confusionNotes: Marbled scuds are easily confused with their close relative Jassa falcata, another tube-building scud. The key difference is the marbled scud's distinctive reddish-brown markings on grey - if you see clear marbling patterns, you've found the marbled species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'scuds,' these marine amphipods are different from the freshwater scuds that many people know from ponds and streams. The name 'amphipod' means 'different feet' because they have several types of legs for different purposes - swimming, walking, and grasping.
compareHints: Since this is the only Jassa species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other small tube-building marine creatures. Unlike barnacles, marbled scuds have visible segmented bodies and can move in and out of their tubes. Unlike small mussels, their tubes are made of debris rather than smooth shell material and have an irregular, bumpy texture.
